files.patch:
@@ -771,6 +771,42 @@ def resolve_entity(context, base, system_id, public_id):
         self.assertEqual(handler_call_args, [("bar", "baz")])
 
 
+class ParentParserLifetimeTest(unittest.TestCase):
+    """
+    Subparsers make use of their parent XML_Parser inside of Expat.
+    As a result, parent parsers need to outlive subparsers.
+
+    See https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139400.
+    """
+
+    def test_parent_parser_outlives_its_subparsers__single(self):
+        parser = expat.ParserCreate()
+        subparser = parser.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
+
+        # Now try to cause garbage collection of the parent parser
+        # while it's still being referenced by a related subparser.
+        del parser
+
+    def test_parent_parser_outlives_its_subparsers__multiple(self):
+        parser = expat.ParserCreate()
+        subparser_one = parser.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
+        subparser_two = parser.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
+
+        # Now try to cause garbage collection of the parent parser
+        # while it's still being referenced by a related subparser.
+        del parser
+
+    def test_parent_parser_outlives_its_subparsers__chain(self):
+        parser = expat.ParserCreate()
+        subparser = parser.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
+        subsubparser = subparser.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
+
+        # Now try to cause garbage collection of the parent parsers
+        # while they are still being referenced by a related subparser.
+        del parser
+        del subparser
+
+
 class ReparseDeferralTest(unittest.TestCase):
     def test_getter_setter_round_trip(self):
         parser = expat.ParserCreate()

@@ -0,0 +1,4 @@
+:mod:`xml.parsers.expat`: Make sure that parent Expat parsers are only
+garbage-collected once they are no longer referenced by subparsers created
+by :meth:`~xml.parsers.expat.xmlparser.ExternalEntityParserCreate`.
+Patch by Sebastian Pipping.

> (@ZeroIntensity how do we usually check this elsewhere? do we use gc.collect() and something like gc.get_referrers? or something like that?)

We usually try to avoid requiring that things get deallocated in tests, because the logic to do so is fragile (for example, deferred reference counting might delay deallocation until a garbage collection). Leaking objects will be picked up in refleak mode anyway.

review_comments.body: @picnixz will do :+1:

> I think you should also visit self->parent to break possible reference cycles.

@picnixz could you elaborate on "visit" and "possible reference cycles"? I don't see a source for cycles yet.

It's possible to create cycles as follows:

```py
import pyexpat as expat

p = expat.ParserCreate()
s = p.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
func = lambda *a, **kw: None; func.s = s; func.p = p; func.t = type(p);
p.ExternalEntityRefHandler = func
p.Parse("<xml></xml>", True)
```

Run the above script with `-X showrefcount` and you'll see leaking blocks. If you add a `Py_VISIT(self->parent);` you'll be able to break reference cycles here.

> The type documents what the parent is, hopefully communicating why it is there (or at least helping that mission).

In this case, I would prefer a comment. Note that strictly speaking, we won't need to access the parent parser except for holding a reference to it right? so a `PyObject *` is fine. 

(Note that in general, we prefer erasing types and use `PyObject *` when we don't need to access its members. Most of the code base I've seen does it like that since it allows to directly use the C API without making un-necessary casts beforehand but it's not always good if you need to access the struct members more than you need to use the C API).

> Note that in general, we prefer erasing types and use PyObject * when we don't need to access its members.

@picnixz that :arrow_up: is the key sentence to me. I will adjust it now…

@picnixz I would like to emphasize that our key problem is that the parent is freed to soon while circles seem to be a topic of "freed later than necessary"(?)… but I'm definatley not understanding your point fully, I have no prior knowledge of `Py_VISIT`. Are we talking functions `xmlparse_traverse` and `xmlparse_clear` here? If you are sure what to do, could you provide instructions on a patch or share a patch file to apply on top? I was not able to run anything with `-X showrefcount`, I would need detailed instructions on that front too. Thanks in advance!
@picnixz applied. How about now?

> Are we talking functions xmlparse_traverse and xmlparse_clear here? 

Yes. Without visiting we would actually never free the memory because there will be a cycle of objects referencing each others. If the cycle is isolated (i.e. all objects in the cycle are never referenced by other objects, we can entirely deallocate the objects in this cycle). But to know whether an object is part of a cycle or not, we need to call this `Py_VISIT` function.

What I meant is:

- Copy my example in some 'test.py'
- Run `./python -X showrefcount test.py`
- Without a `Py_VISIT(self->parent)` call in `xmlparse_traverse`, you'll see leaking blocks. If you add it, you'll see that the memory is properly freed.
- Now, I don't know if a `Py_CLEAR(self->parent)` is really needed in `xmlparse_clear`. We could be clearing `parent` to early if we do it in `Py_CLEAR` as other objects may still be referencing, but I wasn't able to produce a crash. However, considering that the parent parser is a strong reference, I think we should indeed clear it in `xmlparse_clear` (but we don't need to do it in `xmlparse_dealloc` as it calls `xmlparse_clear()`).

```suggestion
    /*
     * Strong reference to a parent `xmlparseobject` if this parser
     * is a child parser. Set to NULL if this parser is a root parser.
     * This is needed to keep the parent parser alive as long as it has
     * at least one child parser.
     *
     * See https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/139400 for details.
     */
    PyObject *parent;
```

(I personally prefer comments above as it's easier to update them rather than aligned ones when the text is too long).

review_comments.body:
Can you add a test where multiple subparsers are created? and also a subparser that create a subparser (I'm not sure it's possible though).

Also, I would like you to add the small repro I gave you where I add a reference cycle so that refleak buildbots can catch any regression there. To summarize:

- 1 test where parser.ExternalEntityParserCreate() is called multiple times.
- 1 test with `subparser` creating a subparser as well.
- 1 test where a subparser is referencing itself in a dummy handler function attached to the parent parser or to another subparser.

I can write the tests for you if you want though but not today.

`tp_clear` is actually meant for also breaking reference cycles. I think we still need to clear it in `tp_clear`. The docs also advise this approach: https://docs.python.org/dev/c-api/typeobj.html#c.PyTypeObject.tp_clear

> tp_clear does not need to delete references to objects that can’t participate in reference cycles, such as Python strings or Python integers. However, it may be convenient to clear all references, and write the type’s [tp_dealloc](https://docs.python.org/dev/c-api/typeobj.html#c.PyTypeObject.tp_dealloc) function to invoke tp_clear to avoid code duplication. (Beware that tp_clear might have already been called. Prefer calling idempotent functions like [Py_CLEAR()](https://docs.python.org/dev/c-api/refcounting.html#c.Py_CLEAR).)

If `tp_clear` cannot break the reference cycle, then we may have objects that can never be collected. I suspect that we could have such situation when involving multiple subparsers with handlers containing references to themselves or their parent parsers.
It's fine. It's a non-trivial reason why we have it and I prefer being explicit here since the project is touched by many people.

@picnixz I think you are speaking of `xmlparse_clear`? If we add `Py_CLEAR(self->parent);` to `xmlparse_clear` (1) we need to drop it from `xmlparse_dealloc` or that will effectively decrement twice and (2) we would decrement the parent before a call to `XML_ParserFree` on the subparser which is not safe *if* the garbage collector can run in parallel and already pick up the parent (a race condition). PS: Moving the call to `xmlparse_clear` past `XML_ParserFree` gets me into new use-after-free situations — not sure why —, so a move of `Py_CLEAR(self->parent);` seems non-trivial. How do you suggest we proceed about this?

review_comments.body: @picnixz I'll make a start for the next push…

> I think you are speaking of xmlparse_clear

Yes sorry, `tp_clear` is the generic name of the slot.

> (1) we need to drop it from xmlparse_dealloc or that will effectively decrement twice 

`Py_CLEAR` is a no-op on NULL objects so that wouldn't cause an issue strictly speaking, but it would better not to.

> we would decrement the parent before a call to XML_ParserFree on the subparser which is not safe if the garbage collector can run in parallel and already pick up the parent (a race condition).

AFAIK, we don't run the GC in parallel. I'm not sure we can have race conditions during traversal/clears (@ZeroIntensity maybe you know anything about this?)

> Moving the call to xmlparse_clear past XML_ParserFree gets me into new use-after-free situations

That's because `xmlparse_clear` clears the handlers (decref them), then it sets the parser's handlers to NULL, so `xmlparse_clear` still requires the Expat parser to exist (so it cannot be after `XML_ParserFree`).

But after what you said, I really wondered whether we can move `Py_CLEAR` inside `tp_clear`. It entirely depends if the parent can be picked up beforehand. I never had this kind of situation beforehand so the problem is indeed non-trivial.

>  I'm not sure we can have race conditions during traversal/clears (@ZeroIntensity maybe you know anything about this?)

We don't run the GC in parallel. On the free-threaded build, we temporarily pause all other threads to run the GC, and on the GIL-icious build, only one thread can access the GC at a time anyway. In other words, it's completely safe to assume that only one thread has access to data in a `tp_traverse` function.

@picnixz maybe there is a simpler way to look at function `xmlparse_clear`: while it's running, `self->itself` — the `XML_Parser` instance — is always set from what I can see. As long as that parser is present, we cannot decrease the parent reference count hence `xmlparse_clear` just cannot do `Py_CLEAR(self->parent);`. Maybe it's as simple as that?

@picnixz PS: Could you share what the remaining open questions or worries are as of today? I'd be happy to help unblock this merge somehow if I can, but I'm not fully sure what it takes at the moment. Thanks! :pray:

Sorry for not replying sooner. I think you're indeed correct and that `Py_CLEAR` should be deferred to `dealloc`. Would you be willing to add a comment in `xmlparse_clear` indicating this for posterity please?

review_comments.body:
My intent was to just create a test where we would have possible of cycles. The simplest way to create cycles is to have something that references itself. Since it's not possible to mutate the type itself, I suggested that the handler creates the cycle itself. The handlers are callables and when we call `Py_VISIT`, the default visitor function would visit their attributes, and one of these attributes would be the parser that we stored.

But I'm not entirely sure that my reasoning here is accurate. At least, that's how I always dealt with reference cycles and how I detected crashes, mostly by adding attributes that have references to the object or its type I'm trying to free.

Possibility one: use the following snippet:

```py
import pyexpat as expat

p = expat.ParserCreate()
s = p.ExternalEntityParserCreate(None)
func = lambda *a, **kw: None
func.s = s
func.p = p
func.t = type(p)
p.StartElementHandler = func
p.Parse("<xml></xml>", True)
```

I think this should be enough to create cycles. But since I don't know how to check this (using gc in tests is not advised in general), the second possibility is to remove this test and investigate more later (I would appreciate if we had a debug option to see the cyclic isolates that the GC finds).
